Regarding the definition of "zero-shot generalization" in the context of text-to-image AIs, it seems sensible. The concept of zero-shot generalization refers to the ability of a model to apply its learned knowledge to new, unseen concepts without requiring additional training data. In the context of text-to-image AIs, this means that the model can generate images based on text prompts without having seen the specific images or concepts before.

The 2013 paper cited in the response likely discussed the theoretical foundations of zero-shot generalization in AI, and its application to text-to-image AIs is a natural extension of this concept. Zero-shot generalization is a desirable property in AI models, as it enables them to generalize to new, unseen data without requiring extensive retraining.

However, it's worth noting that achieving zero-shot generalization in text-to-image AIs is a challenging task, as it requires the model to have a deep understanding of the underlying concepts and relationships between text and images. The model must be able to recognize patterns and relationships in the data, and apply this knowledge to generate coherent and relevant images.
